solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Criminal's demand to pass drink

parts.note: to pass something to someone is to hand it over
to sup is to drink in small mouthfuls

explanation.surface: A villain insists on being handed a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'to pass drink' the content of the demand; it is really two verbs placed side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A robber holding someone up with a gun orders them to raise their arms with this stock phrase.

clue.text: A passage of Beethoven in coastal resort

indicators.note: a passage is a section of text, so a stretch of letters is lifted from the composer's name

parts.note: the composer's name contains the town's four letters running consecutively in its middle

explanation.surface: A seaside town features in a piece of Beethoven's music.
explanation.walkthrough: Hove is a seaside town beside Brighton on England's south coast. 'Passage' poses as a musical extract.
explanation.definitionFit: Hove is a seaside town in East Sussex, now part of the city of Brighton and Hove.

clue.text: For a number, the setter leaves four and nine out

definitions.note: read as numb-er, something that numbs

indicators.note: the remaining letters are put out of order and rearranged
the setter's letter departs from the two number words

parts.note: the number word taken as written
the number word taken as written
the crossword setter refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: An instruction for a number puzzle about removing digits.
explanation.walkthrough: Nurofen is a British brand of ibuprofen painkiller. 'Number' looks like a figure but is something that numbs.
explanation.definitionFit: A painkiller dulls sensation, so it is jokingly a 'numb-er', a numbing agent sold under that brand.

clue.text: Descendant of dissolute cousin not upper-class

indicators.note: a dissolute life is loose and disordered, so the letters are disordered
the upper-class letter is removed from cousin

parts.note: the relative's word taken as written, to be reduced and jumbled
U was coined for upper-class usage, as in 'U and non-U'

explanation.surface: A family member's heir is a debauched relative from a lower class.
explanation.definitionFit: A scion is an heir or younger member of a family, literally a shoot grafted from a plant.

clue.text: Proper English throne overturned from long ago

parts.note: prim means stiffly proper

indicators.note: in a down answer the toilet word is turned upside down

parts.note: throne is jokey slang for the toilet, a lav

explanation.surface: An English monarch is properly deposed in ancient times.
explanation.walkthrough: Lav, short for lavatory, is British for the toilet. 'Throne' suggests royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Primeval means belonging to the earliest ages of the world, so dating from the distant past.

clue.text: Heroically resisting pizzicato, perhaps?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: not defeated or submitting, standing proud
second meaning, read literally: played without a bow, as a plucked string passage is

explanation.walkthrough: Pizzicato means plucking a violin's strings rather than bowing them, so such playing is whimsically 'un-bowed'; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: The ordinary adjective describes someone still upright and defiant after attack, never bending in surrender.

clue.text: Wanting education and mostly ill prepared

indicators.note: all but the final letter of the word is kept

parts.note: unready means not prepared

explanation.surface: Someone is poorly schooled and largely unprepared for an exam.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unread has not done much reading, so lacks book learning; the adjective means uneducated.

clue.text: Rings head of theatre as well as players here

parts.note: a band is a ring, such as a wedding band

indicators.note: the first letter of theatre leads

parts.note: the word whose opening letter is used
and adds things together just as this phrase does

explanation.surface: Phoning the theatre director along with the cast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Players' sounds like the cast of the theatre just mentioned; it means musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandstand is an outdoor platform, often in a park, where a band of musicians performs.

clue.text: Hopeful prohibition gets lifted during decline

indicators.note: the reversed ban comes in the course of the declining word

parts.note: to wane is to decline, as the moon does

indicators.note: in a down answer the word is raised, so read from bottom to top

parts.note: a ban prohibits something

explanation.surface: A ban is repealed while its support is falling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' sounds like repeal of the prohibition; in a down answer it means reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A hopeful is an aspirant hoping to succeed, which is exactly what a wannabe is, a would-be.

clue.text: Put off some food — consumed sandwiches last for dinner

parts.note: a dish is a portion of prepared food

indicators.note: the eaten word encloses the next letter like bread around a filling

parts.note: eaten means consumed

indicators.note: only the final letter of dinner is taken

parts.note: the word whose final letter is used

explanation.surface: Food eaten in sandwiches at the end of dinner proves off-putting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' and 'food' make a meal of it, but 'sandwiches' is a verb signalling one piece placed inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: To dishearten is to discourage, causing someone to lose spirit, like putting them off.

clue.text: Person checking lines succeeded as a linesman?

definitions.note: a whimsical description of a poet, a man who produces lines of verse

parts.note: a verifier is someone who checks things, here lines of text

explanation.surface: A proofreader moves up to become a football official.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the genealogical abbreviation for succeeded. 'Linesman' looks like the football official; the question mark tells you it means a maker of poetic lines.
explanation.definitionFit: A versifier writes verse, composed of lines, so playfully he is a man of lines.

clue.text: Roman's date is not a bit small

parts.note: none means not any at all, as in 'none the wiser'

explanation.surface: Someone asks a Roman's girlfriend whether she is petite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Date' suggests a romantic partner; it is a calendar day.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the nones was a named day of each month, the ninth day before the ides.

clue.text: European and say a pair of Poles bring round Irishman's work

parts.note: a Finn is a native of Finland
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means when introducing an instance
taken as written
N and S, the north and south poles
to wake someone is to bring them round from sleep

explanation.surface: A European and two Polish people try to revive someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' with a capital looks like people from Poland; it means the two magnetic poles. The Irishman is James Joyce.
explanation.definitionFit: Finnegans Wake is the famously difficult final novel by the Irish writer James Joyce.

clue.text: Beat Iris and Ethel gutlessly on behind

parts.note: the yellow flag is a species of wild iris

indicators.note: with its insides removed, only the outer letters of Ethel remain

parts.note: the name from which only the first and last letters survive
running behind schedule is being late

explanation.surface: Two women, Iris and Ethel, are cowardly and lagging at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: Iris and Ethel read as women's names; the first is the flower, the second gets gutted.
explanation.definitionFit: To flagellate is to flog or whip someone, which is to beat them.

clue.text: Pine and willow casing old vessel

parts.note: to long for something is to pine for it

indicators.note: the bat is wrapped around the letter for old, like a case around its contents

parts.note: cricket bats are made of willow, so the wood stands for the bat

explanation.surface: Two kinds of tree wood are used to clad an ancient boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' and 'willow' look like a pair of timbers; one is a verb meaning yearn, the other a cricket bat.
explanation.definitionFit: A longboat is a large rowing boat, famously the Viking ship, so it is a kind of seagoing craft.

clue.text: See guy turning up around store, in charge

indicators.note: the reversed word sits around the store
in a down answer the teasing word is read upwards

parts.note: to guy someone is to tease them, as is to rib them
a shop is a store

explanation.surface: Seeing a man arrive around the shop to take charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like the verb; it is a bishop's diocese, as in the Holy See.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is the area governed by a bishop, which is also called the bishopric or diocese.

clue.text: Zoom call only half about head of state

indicators.note: just the first half of the four-letter word call is kept

parts.note: the word whose first half is used
ER, Elizabeth Regina, was the British head of state

explanation.surface: A Zoom call is cut short because a head of state interrupts.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen, Britain's head of state. 'Zoom' looks like the video app but is the verb to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: To career is to move headlong at great speed, just as to zoom is.

clue.text: Bound to be in extremely terrible, indebted state

indicators.note: the outer letters of terrible are to stand where the word in stands

parts.note: in the red means overdrawn or in debt
the little word in itself, the part of the indebted phrase being swapped out

indicators.note: only the letters at the extremes of terrible are used

parts.note: the word whose two extreme letters are used

explanation.surface: Someone is sure to be in a dreadfully indebted condition.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as an instruction: the ends of terrible are to be the word 'in' within the phrase meaning overdrawn, replacing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tethered is tied up with a rope or chain, just as something bound is.

clue.text: Going around a lake, my waterproof covering

indicators.note: the exclamation surrounds the other letters as a walker might circle a lake

parts.note: 'my!' and 'gosh!' are both exclamations of surprise
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone walking round a lake is glad of their waterproof shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks possessive but is the exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: A galosh is a rubber overshoe worn over ordinary shoes to keep them dry in the wet.

clue.text: Something for a baby, a little poem?

parts.note: a lay is a short narrative poem or song
-ette is the diminutive suffix, as in kitchenette

explanation.surface: A gift for an infant: perhaps a short nursery rhyme?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'a little poem' is a playful build of the word from its pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A layette is a set of clothes, bedding and other items prepared for a newborn child.

clue.text: Laughter about a scoundrel initially alleviating back pain

indicators.note: the laughter wraps around the rest

parts.note: he-he is a written giggle

indicators.note: the scoundrel and the letter that follows are read from right to left

parts.note: a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably

indicators.note: only the opening letter of alleviating is used

parts.note: the word whose opening letter is used

explanation.surface: Having a laugh about a rogue helps ease backache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back pain' reads as one ailment; 'back' is the reversal signal and 'pain' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A headache is a pain in the head, and figuratively any troublesome nuisance.

clue.text: Did quail or chicken, we hear

indicators.note: the answer is pronounced like the cowardly word

parts.note: a chicken is slang for a coward

explanation.surface: A choice between two game birds, quail or chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: Quail and chicken both look like birds; both are really about fear.
explanation.definitionFit: To quail is to shrink back in fear, and cowered is the past tense of crouching in terror.

clue.text: Spinning plate, one lacks civilised instincts

definitions.note: read as 'one that lacks', a noun phrase

indicators.note: spinning turns the plate round so its letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a lamina is a thin plate or layer

explanation.surface: A circus plate-spinner is a lone uncivilised brute.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a person an animal means they are brutish, governed by base urges rather than manners.

clue.text: Wager miserable rozzers are authoritarian

parts.note: to lay a bet is to wager
down means low in spirits
British slang for the police, also called the law

explanation.surface: Betting that unhappy police officers are a bossy lot.
explanation.walkthrough: Rozzers is old British slang for police officers, collectively 'the law'.
explanation.definitionFit: People who issue firm commands and expect obedience are said to dictate rules in this idiom.

clue.text: Italian bear touring island by India

indicators.note: the carrying word goes around the island letter, like a traveller touring it

parts.note: to lug is to carry or bear something heavy
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An Italian bear goes on tour around an island near India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the animal; it is a verb meaning carry.
explanation.definitionFit: Luigi is a common Italian man's given name, so an example of an Italian person.

clue.text: Sports champion remains after burning energy

parts.note: ash is what is left after a fire

explanation.surface: A sports star burns out, leaving only the ashes of their energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ashe won Wimbledon in 1975, the first Black man to win it.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe was an American tennis player who won three Grand Slam singles titles.

clue.text: Post or beam with one end knocked off

indicators.note: the beam loses its opening letter, as if a carpenter sawed off one end

parts.note: a rafter is a sloping roof beam

explanation.surface: A wooden post or beam damaged at one end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Post' looks like a timber upright beside 'beam'; it is the prefix-word meaning later than.
explanation.definitionFit: Post as in post-war means following in time, a Latin-derived synonym of the plain preposition.

clue.text: It precedes fast run in dip by one tot heading west

indicators.note: in an across answer, going west means reading right to left
the run letter goes inside the dip

parts.note: a sag is a dip or droop
I is the Roman numeral one
a dram is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: A sequence of a dip, a run and a drink, like a sports or pub routine.
explanation.walkthrough: R is the cricket abbreviation for run. 'Fast' looks like speed but means abstaining from food.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrove Tuesday, the carnival day, comes immediately before the Lent abstinence begins on Ash Wednesday.

clue.text: Examining body stand out, holding drape at edges

indicators.note: the larger word contains the shorter piece within it

parts.note: to excel is to stand out as superior

indicators.note: only the outermost letters of drape are taken

parts.note: the curtain word whose outside letters are used

explanation.surface: An inspector's body stands out, wrapped in a curtain.
explanation.walkthrough: Edexcel is a British exam board setting GCSEs and A levels. 'Examining body' sounds like a post-mortem on a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: Edexcel is one of England's main awarding organisations, which set and mark school qualifications.

clue.text: Peter out in gusty weather getting led astray outside

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit around the weather word
the letters of led wander off course into a new order

parts.note: the word taken as written, then scrambled
wind is weather that comes in gusts

explanation.surface: Someone loses their way in a gale and their energy fades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' looks like a name; peter out is a phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwindle is to diminish gradually until little or nothing is left, the sense of the phrasal verb.
